# Measured results

No accuracy or performance numbers are claimed for kore-self on real data.
A number may be quoted elsewhere only if it has a row here with: n, baseline, interval, date, commit.

**Every number below comes from synthetic data** generated by `kore-self/src/synth.rs`
(Poisson topic counts, uniform and planted-probability actions, phrases written by the
same author as the detectors). They show how the rule-based detectors behave on data
that matches their assumptions. They are not real-life accuracy, and real logs will
be burstier, messier and phrased differently.

| Claim | n | baseline | interval | date | commit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Habit detection precision (Wilson lower bound >= 0.5, min n 8), synthetic | 20 seeds x 3 noise levels, 3 true habits + 3 non-habit contexts per seed | none (truth known) | 1.00 at every seed and noise level | 2026-10-23 | f8440c8a |
| Habit detection recall, synthetic, 0% / 20% / 50% noise | 20 seeds each | none | mean 1.00 / 0.85 / 0.43; per-seed range 1.00-1.00 / 0.67-1.00 / 0.00-0.67 | 2026-10-23 | f8440c8a |
| Topic change point recall (match within 7 days), synthetic | 20 seeds x 3 planted changes, per noise level | none | mean 0.97 / 0.93 / 0.90 at 0 / 20 / 50% noise; per-seed range 0.67-1.00 | 2026-10-23 | f8440c8a |
| Topic change point precision, synthetic | same runs | none | median 1.00; per-seed range 0.67-1.00 (0%), 0.50-1.00 (20%), 0.67-1.00 (50%) | 2026-10-23 | f8440c8a |
| Change point false-positive rate (unchanged topic flagged), synthetic | 20 seeds x 5 steady topics = 100 series per noise level | none | pooled mean 0.010 at every noise level (1 of 100); per-seed max 0.20 | 2026-10-23 | f8440c8a |
| Change point detection delay (days after the planted change until a prefix of the data first shows it) | detected changes of 20 seeds | none | mean 7.7 / 7.8 / 9.1 days at 0 / 20 / 50% noise; per-seed range 5.0-12.3 / 5.0-15.0 / 5.0-20.0 | 2026-10-23 | f8440c8a |

## How to reproduce

```
cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_learning --offline --release
cargo test -p kore-self --offline        # includes measured_detector_quality_on_synthetic_data_stays_above_floor
```

Seeds 1..=20, noise 0.0 / 0.2 / 0.5, default parameters
`{"habit_min_n":8,"habit_lb":0.5,"habit_window_days":0,"change_llr":12.0,"change_min_seg":10,"change_min_ratio":1.8,"change_min_total":10,"habit_lift":0.0,"habit_max_share":0.9}` (the two lift parameters were added after the tagged table was first recorded; the tagged table is unchanged by them, see "Tagged lives after the fix").
Each synthetic life is 150 days from 2024-01-01 with about 2000-3000 events. Noise adds
that fraction of extra events: 40% random actions inside the habit contexts (which
dilutes the habits), 40% random topic mentions (which flattens topic shifts), 20% chatter,
including near-miss phrases ("They now prefer coffee for work.", "I prefer tea for
mornings.", "If I now prefer ...").

Actual output of the run (median [min-max] over the 20 seeds):

## Definitions

* Habit truth: planted (context, action) with probability >= 0.6 (three per life: 0.9, 0.8, 0.7).
  Non-habit contexts: one weak planted action (p = 0.35) and two uniform contexts.
  Habit recall falls with noise because the injected random actions pull a planted
  rate such as 0.7 toward the 0.5 bound; that is the detector refusing to call it a habit, and
  it is the main behaviour the evolution loop can tune (lower `habit_lb`).
* Change point match: same topic and detected day within 7 days of the planted day.
  Precision = matched detections / all detections; recall = matched planted changes / planted changes.
  Delay is measured by re-running the detector on the data truncated day by day.
* Stance: event-level. The cited event must be a planted statement; key accuracy checks the topic.
  The distractor phrases and the matcher were written by the same author, so 1.00 says the matcher
  follows its own grammar, not that it understands real writing.
* min-n refusal: the share of planted tiny contexts that were refused.

## Test floors

The test `measured_detector_quality_on_synthetic_data_stays_above_floor` (in
`kore-self/src/learn_tests.rs`) fails if a run drops below slightly under the floor measured
above: habit precision >= 0.95; stance precision, recall and key accuracy >= 0.95; min-n
refusal >= 0.95; change precision >= 0.45, recall >= 0.6, per-seed FP rate <= 0.25, date
error <= 5 days; habit recall >= 0.95 (0% noise), >= 0.6 (20%), median >= 0.3 (50%).
These thresholds guard against regressions on synthetic data; they are not accuracy claims.

## Evolution loop: one example, not a measurement

`self_evolve_rules` on the end-to-end test's synthetic life (seed 11, 20% noise, 150 days, cut date
2024-04-14, 4 selection origins, 5 evaluation origins, horizon 14 days, margin 0.02) proposed
`habit_lb` 0.5 -> 0.4 (13 candidates tried). Next-period habit F1 on the evaluation origins:
candidate 0.929, incumbent 0.870, trivial baseline 0.491; verdict promoted
(code at commit f8440c8a; see README "Learning quick start"). This is one run on
one synthetic life and says nothing about other data. Whether the loop helps across seeds has
not been measured.

## Free-text lives with keyword rules (synthetic, author-written templates)

Same detectors, same 20 seeds, same noise levels and parameters, but the synthetic life is
written as short journal sentences with no tags (`synth::free_text_config`) and read
through the keyword rules `synth::free_text_rules()` (the same format as a user's
`tag_rules.txt`). **The sentence templates, the distractors and the keyword rules were all written by
the same author, in one sitting, knowing each other.** The numbers say how the rule layer behaves on text that was
written to be mostly matchable, with these deliberate difficulties: varied phrasing
(3-4 templates per context, action and topic); 40% of the occasions that did not take
a planted habit mention it negated ("did not run at all", "skipped the podcast"), 15% of those
as post-negations the guard cannot see ("the run was called off"); 10% of real actions and
topic mentions use a synonym the rules do not list ("did laps around the track");
keyword-bearing distractors in the noise ("The bus ran late again.", "My reading glasses broke.").
They are not accuracy on anyone's real journal.

How occasions are counted (code: `learn/habits.rs`, docs in `learn/tagrules.rs`): a keyword
context is an occasion for each event with a sentence matching it, and the action counts if its
keywords match in the same sentence; the built-in `weekday`/`weekend` contexts are day-level
(every day with an event; the action counts if any event of the day matches).

### What was wrong at first, and the fix

The first version of this section (commit 5d45ece3) reported overall habit precision 0.50 / 0.29 / 0.00 (median at 0 / 20 / 50% noise),
with 1 to 12 false habits per life in the built-in `weekday` / `weekend` contexts. Cause: the synthetic life has about 15 events a day
and no weekday structure, so an action such as `run` occurs on 60-70% of weekdays *and* on 60-70% of weekend days. A context that holds on
almost every unit gives every frequent action a high in-context rate, and the Wilson bound alone cannot tell "the action's base rate"
from "a habit of this context". (An even earlier variant that treated keyword contexts day-level too gave mean precision 0.21 at 0% noise
for the same reason and was replaced by sentence-level occasions.)

The fix (`habits::detect_full`, parameters in the rule set, see README "Free-text journals"):

1. **Lift test** (`habit_lift`, default 0.0): the in-context Wilson lower bound must exceed the Wilson upper bound of the same action's
   rate in all *other* contexts of the same family (stored tags, built-in date contexts, keyword contexts) plus the margin. For weekday the
   comparison is exactly the weekend. A negative value switches the test off. With fewer than `habit_min_n` out-of-context occasions the
   test cannot be made and the habit is kept (a log with a single context has nothing to compare with).
2. **Uninformative contexts** (`habit_max_share`, default 0.9): a rule-derived context that holds on more than this share of its units
   (days for weekday/weekend, events for keyword contexts) is dropped and reported (`uninformative_contexts` in `self_learn`).
3. Min-n refusal is unchanged and comes first.

The defaults are the principled values (a margin of zero, the 90% suggested in advance), not fitted. Parameter choices were looked at on
tuning seeds 101..120 only (never on the reported seeds 1..20): on those seeds the free-text overall habit precision was median 1.00 with
per-seed minimum 0.75 / 0.67 / 0.00 at 0 / 20 / 50% noise (0.00 where nothing planted was detected and one false habit existed), and a median of 0
built-in-context habits per life (maximum 1). So a residual false habit does occur on some lives; on the reported seeds none did.

Before the fix (same seeds): overall habit precision 0.50 / 0.29 / 0.00 and 2 / 5 / 9 built-in-context habits per life (medians); everything else in the table is
identical before and after (habit recall, change columns, stance columns), so the fix removed false habits without costing planted-habit recall on these data.

Reading the table honestly:

* Overall habit precision is now 1.00 at every seed. Caveats: (a) at 50% noise most lives detect no planted habit at all (recall 0.07), and the harness
  prints a precision of "nothing detected" as 1.00, so that cell is vacuous; (b) the tuning seeds showed that false habits do not vanish entirely
  (see above); (c) the planted contexts were never at risk from the lift test here because the other contexts use different actions, so these data do not show
  what the lift test costs when a true habit shares its action with other contexts (it would be refused, by design).
* Habit recall (planted habits found, 3 per life) is unchanged and falls with noise like the tagged table, plus loss from unlisted synonyms and unseen
  post-negations: mean 0.93 / 0.70 / 0.07 at 0 / 20 / 50% noise versus 1.00 / 0.85 / 0.43 for tagged lives. Precision recovered; recall did not improve and is still poor at 50% noise.
* Topic change detection is slightly worse than with tags (mean recall 0.92 / 0.90 / 0.88 versus 0.97 / 0.93 / 0.90; delay 8.2 / 9.1 / 10.1 days
  versus 7.7 / 7.8 / 9.1) because 10% of mentions use unlisted words. Its false-positive rate is 1 or 2 of 100 unchanged series.
* Stances never used tags, so they are unchanged (the same-author caveat above applies).

### Tagged lives after the fix

The lift test applies to stored-tag contexts too (family "stored tags"). Re-measured on seeds 1..20 the tagged table printed above in this file is identical to the
table before the change in every cell (habit precision 1.00 [1.00-1.00], recall 1.00 / 0.85 / 0.43 means, and the rest): in these lives each planted habit's action is
rare in the other contexts, so the lift test refuses nothing. Existing tagged revisions are not rewritten (their rationale text is unchanged); only the
numbers and a new `out_of_context` field in the `self_learn` detail are added.

Test floors for this section (`free_text_measured_quality_stays_above_floor`, set slightly under the minima above):
overall and planted-context habit precision >= 0.95; at most 1 built-in-context habit per life; stance precision and recall >= 0.95; min-n refusal >= 0.95;
change precision >= 0.3 and recall >= 0.3 per seed; change false-positive rate <= 0.25; date error <= 6 days;
habit recall >= 0.6 (0% noise, per-seed minimum) and median >= 0.5 (20%). There is deliberately no floor for habit recall at 50% noise.

Not measured for free text: any real journal; synonyms or sentences written by someone other than the rule author;
`negation = all`; the evolution loop and ledger on free text beyond a functional test (they now read `tag_rules.txt`
like `self_learn`, `evolve_and_ledger_use_the_same_virtual_tags_as_learn`; their scores on free-text lives are not measured).

## Being loop: chooser in a simulated world (synthetic world, author-defined rewards)

Everything here comes from `kore-self/src/being/` (a deterministic simulated world; no real data). The tasks (arithmetic, linear equations, physics formulas, sequences), the costs, the rewards and the scripted solvers were all written by the same author. The being's "preference" for a domain is produced by those defined rewards (reward points per energy unit spent); the numbers say how well the UCB1 chooser finds the best-paying domain in this world, not anything about general ability.

Setup: 20 worlds (world seeds 1..20, the report seeds); each world has a hidden profile (reward scale, base cost, difficulty mix per domain) derived from its seed. Every policy gets the same budget of 600 energy units (about 99 steps) and the same tasks at the same step. "oracle" is told the domain with the best expected reward per energy (estimated by 3000 sampled tasks); it can still be beaten in a single world by luck. The exploration constant of the chooser (0.05) was chosen on separate tuning seeds 101..120 (c in 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.5; 0.05 gave the highest mean reward per energy there, 1.93 against an oracle of 2.12). Intervals are 95% t-intervals of the mean over the 20 worlds. Run `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_being --offline --release` (2026-10-24, commit 55dc05f7).

| policy | mean reward per energy unit | 95% interval of the mean | per-world range |
|---|---|---|---|
| random domain | 1.295 | [1.167, 1.424] | 0.896-1.937 |
| always arithmetic | 1.650 | [1.416, 1.883] | 0.849-2.399 |
| always algebra | 1.467 | [1.302, 1.631] | 0.866-2.240 |
| always physics | 0.627 | [0.467, 0.788] | 0.328-1.495 |
| always pattern | 1.525 | [1.325, 1.725] | 0.761-2.472 |
| oracle (hidden best domain) | 1.902 | [1.702, 2.102] | 1.102-2.472 |
| learned chooser (UCB1) | 1.694 | [1.512, 1.876] | 1.050-2.370 |

Hidden best domain over the 20 report worlds: arithmetic 10, algebra 3, physics 0, pattern 7.

| quantity (report seeds 1..20) | mean | 95% interval of the mean | range |
|---|---|---|---|
| regret per energy, learned vs oracle | 0.208 | [0.087, 0.329] | -0.115 to 0.826 |
| regret per energy, random vs oracle | 0.607 | [0.431, 0.783] | 0.087 to 1.300 |
| total reward in the budget, learned (points) | 1013 | [904, 1122] | 627-1415 |
| total reward in the budget, random (points) | 776 | [699, 854] | 537-1162 |
| share of the learned picks on the best domain, steps 1-30 | 0.49 | [0.35, 0.64] | 0.03-0.87 |
| steps 31-80 | 0.58 | [0.36, 0.79] | 0.00-1.00 |
| step 81 on | 0.50 | [0.27, 0.73] | 0.00-1.00 |
| share of random picks on the best domain | 0.25 | [0.23, 0.27] | 0.18-0.32 |

Reading: the learned chooser earns about 31% more reward per energy than random choice (1.69 against 1.30; learned beat random in 18 of 20 worlds) and closes about two thirds of the gap between random and the oracle (regret 0.21 against 0.61). It is NOT better than the best fixed domain on average: always-arithmetic scored 1.65 and the learned chooser beat it in only 8 of 20 worlds (always-algebra 11, always-pattern 10, always-physics 20 of 20). It concentrates slowly: in 12 of 20 worlds the trailing 20 picks reached 60% on the best domain at some point (median first at step 20, which is mostly the initial exploration), and the share of picks on the best domain stays near 0.5, because several domains pay almost the same and the roughly 100-step budget leaves little time to separate them. On the tuning seeds the numbers were similar (learned 1.93, random 1.36, oracle 2.12, hidden best: arithmetic 6, algebra 11, pattern 3). The claim is only: under these defined rewards the learned chooser collects more reward per energy than random choice and than always-physics, and about the same as the best single fixed domain.

Other tests (all in `kore-self/src/being/tests.rs`, `tests/e2e_being.rs`): two worlds with different hidden best domains give different preferences, and in each the preferred domain has about the best reward per energy in the being's own log (at least 0.85 of the best logged); the same seeds give a byte-identical log content hash and head hash (with a fixed clock; with the wall clock only `recorded_at` differs); every decision of a 130-step run is re-derived from the log alone and the next decision equals the replayed prediction; a run split over two calls equals one run; a flipped byte after a run fails `self_verify`.

Test floors (set after the measurement, a margin below it): learned minus random mean reward per energy > 0.2 (measured 0.40), regret versus oracle < 0.45 (measured 0.21), learned beats random in at least 15 of 20 worlds (measured 18). Guards against regression, not accuracy claims.

## Track B1: world-model learner in a menu world (synthetic world, author-defined rewards)

Everything here is the same kind of simulation as above: author-written tasks, rewards, costs and solvers, no real data. Track B asks whether a being can learn from its own log which options pay. Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_being --offline --release -- menu` (2026-10-24, branch self-b1, built on commit a0ba7566).

What is new. Each step the world offers a menu of 4 tasks (domain drawn from the world seed, difficulty and listed cost and reward as before); the being picks one task and one of three solver strategies, or skips the menu for 1 energy unit. Strategies: fast (half the listed energy, exact only for difficulty 1-2, a cheap heuristic above, three times the slip rate), careful (the old scripted solver, listed energy), deep (twice the energy, exact on every template, half the slip rate). The old single-task mode and its numbers above are unchanged (the old tests still pass). The learner (`being/model.rs`, `being/planner.rs`) keeps, per (domain, difficulty, strategy), a Beta posterior of the success probability shrunk from the (domain, strategy) estimate, which is shrunk from the strategy-wide estimate (prior strength 4), plus the energy actually spent as a ratio of the listed cost. It is built only from the logged outcomes. The planner scores every (offered task, strategy) as `listed reward x min(1, p + beta x sd) / estimated energy` (UCB on the model, no random numbers, so replay is exact), takes the best affordable one, and skips when that score is below `skip_frac` times the reward per energy it has earned so far. Every decision logs all 12 alternatives with their estimates, uncertainty and scores.

Setup. Report seeds 1..20 (20 worlds), tuning seeds 101..120. Beta and skip_frac were chosen on the tuning seeds only (grid beta in 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3 with skip_frac in 0, 0.3, 0.6, then beta in 1, 1.5, 2, 3 with skip_frac in 0, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, at both budgets; beta 1.5 with skip_frac 1.0 had the best mean over the two budgets: 3.42 at budget 600 and 3.65 at budget 3000 on the tuning seeds, against baselines of about 1.5-2.1 there). Budgets 600 (about 150 attempts) and 3000. Baselines: random over (offer, strategy); greedy by listed reward per listed cost (uses only what is printed on the menu) with the careful strategy, and also with fast always and deep always (the best fixed strategy is the fair comparison, since the old policies cannot choose a strategy); the UCB1 domain chooser (the best old policy: UCB1 over domains, then the best listed ratio in that domain, careful); the oracle (knows the hidden success probability of every strategy and the real energy, never skips). The oracle never skips, so a learner that skips can in principle get close to or above it. Intervals are 95% t-intervals of the mean over the 20 worlds.

Verdict. The model learner beats every baseline in these worlds: +1.5 reward per energy over UCB1 at budget 600 (95% interval +1.2 to +1.8, better in 20 of 20 worlds), +1.1 over the best fixed strategy (greedy with fast, 19 of 20 worlds), and it comes within 0.38 (budget 600) and 0.16 (budget 3000, interval includes 0) of the oracle. Read this with its limits: most of the gap to UCB1 and to greedy-careful comes from choosing a strategy and from skipping, which those policies cannot do; the learner mainly found "use the fast strategy on tasks where it is reliable, skip menus where nothing looks good" (per world at budget 600: 143 fast, 11 careful, 0.3 deep attempts, 36 skips); deep is almost never worth its double energy in this world. The strategies' costs and reliabilities were written by the same author, so this shows the learner finds a good policy in this designed trade-off, not that the policy is generally good. Skipping adds a small gain (+0.17 at budget 600, 19 of 20 worlds; +0.07 at budget 3000, 15 of 20 worlds). The report-seed means are lower than the tuning-seed means (3.12 against 3.42 at budget 600), which is the usual small tuning optimism.

Brier score of the model: 0.0895; Brier of predicting the running overall success rate: 0.1067 (lower is better)

Calibration reading. Every prediction is made before its outcome is seen, so the points are out of sample (this is a one-step-ahead check, not a separate held-out set). The model beats the "predict the running overall success rate" baseline on Brier (0.127 against 0.169 at budget 600; 0.090 against 0.107 at budget 3000). It is overconfident where it predicts 0.2-0.6 (for example predicted 0.45, observed 0.27) and close to the diagonal from 0.6 up; the planner mostly attempts high-probability options, so the low bins hold few attempts (22-153 of 2881 at budget 600) and mostly cells with little evidence. The model's predicted success is also stored as the prediction of each attempt in the log.

Tests (`kore-self/src/being/tests.rs`, `tests/e2e_being.rs`): the menu world is deterministic and the single-task ids are unchanged; every domain has three strategies with the documented cost/reliability trade-off (deep more reliable than fast on hard templates, fast reliable on easy ones); the model folded from the log equals the live model; model.rs and planner.rs mention none of the hidden world fields (source scan); every decision of a 200-step menu run is re-derived from the log alone, with 12 logged alternatives each, and a run split over two calls equals one run; skipped menus are logged without predictions; the chooser is fixed once the being exists; a flipped byte after a model run fails verification; refill replay; the real binary runs the model chooser, explains a decision and keeps the chooser setting. Floors (a margin below the measured values at budget 600, seeds 1..20): model above UCB1 by more than 1.0 (measured 1.52), above greedy-careful and random by more than 1.0, above greedy-fast by more than 0.6 (measured 1.11), regret versus the oracle below 1.0 (measured 0.38), better than UCB1 in at least 18 of 20 worlds (measured 20), Brier below the base-rate Brier; at budget 3000 on seed 3 above UCB1 by more than 0.8. These guard against regression; they are not accuracy claims.

Not measured: worlds whose task mix or strategy trade-offs differ from this design; changing worlds (new domains appearing mid-life); strategies the learner has to discover (step B2); any language-model input (B4); the effect of the hyper-parameters outside the grid above. Changing `DEFAULT_BETA`, `DEFAULT_SKIP_FRAC` or the model's prior strength changes how an existing model-chooser log replays, so they are part of the version of the being.

## Not measured

Real-life data of any kind (the free-text section above is also synthetic); the ledger's probabilities (nothing is scored yet); behaviour with
the being loop in any world other than the author-defined simulation (no real tasks, no language-model thinker); very large logs; sensitivity to the synthetic generator's choices (150 days, Poisson counts).
